setup.zh: 褚先生讲灵根：一门者，天灵根；二门者，真灵根……「五门俱全的，你们叫杂灵根，四面漏风。」满堂哄笑：「漏勺！漏勺！」「沈小满。你说，漏勺能打水吗？」
setup.en: Master Chu lectures on spirit roots: one door, a heavenly root; two doors, a true root… "Five doors complete — that's what you call a mixed root: leaks on every side." The hall roars: "Leaky ladle! Leaky ladle!" "Shen Xiaoman. Tell me — can a leaky ladle carry water?"

recap.zh: 褚先生当堂问你：漏勺能打水吗？你说：能，多打几次。
recap.en: Master Chu asked you before the whole hall whether a leaky ladle can carry water. You said: yes — go back for more.

zh: 褚先生讲灵根，山羊胡子一翘。
「五门俱全的，你们叫杂灵根，四面漏风。」
en: Master Chu lectures on spirit roots; his goatee twitches.
"Five doors complete — that's what you call a mixed root: leaks on every side."
"Shen Xiaoman. Tell me — can a leaky ladle carry water?"

text.zh: 胡子一翘一翘，倒像在替他点头；你暗暗数了，他讲一段，要翘七回。
text.en: The goatee bobs up and down as if nodding for him. You count on the quiet: seven bobs to a passage.

text.zh: 戒尺一头磨得发亮，另一头却新得很——先生打人，只用一头。
text.en: One end of the ruler is worn bright; the other looks new. The master only ever strikes with one end.

story.zh:
讲经堂在正殿东边，隔着一片老柏。左边那扇门上挂着一块刷了白粉的木牌，是课程表。有人念到「四层以上」，回头问：「咱们这一屋子，有四层的么？」没有人答。

头一讲那天，钟敲过了，忽然有人「咦」了一声，指着窗外。一道青光斜斜地落下来，不快，像一片叶子顺着风往下飘。近了，才看清是一个人，脚底下踩着一口剑，一身灰袍叫风鼓起来。他从三重屋脊上头掠过去，屋脊上歇着的一排麻雀一只也没惊起。

他两根手指往回一招，那口剑「铮」地轻吟一声，自己缩回他背后的鞘里；他背着手进了门。满堂一下子没了声。孙二狗嘴张着，半天没合上，末了小声道：「……神仙。」

孙二狗憋了半天，到底问出了口：「褚先生，何时我们才能像您一样，成仙，会飞啊？」褚先生从讲桌上拿起戒尺，在掌心里拍了两下，山羊胡子翘了一翘：「成仙？还早着呢。不过筑基之后，便可御剑飞行，这个倒不难。」满堂的眼睛都亮了。

这便是[褚先生]{注=chuxiansheng}。听说五十来岁了，看着不过三十许，脸上一条褶子也没有。这一院子里，只他一个是筑了基的。踩着一口剑，从云里下来——他心里只剩一句话：这辈子，我也要这么飞上一回。前头几排坐的是真灵根，后头几排坐的是伪灵根、杂灵根。小满坐在最后一排。

褚先生背着手，摇头晃脑地讲道：「一门者，天灵根；二门者，真灵根；三门者，弱灵根；四门者，伪灵根——」山羊胡子一翘，目光不偏不倚停在小满身上，「——五门俱全的，你们叫杂灵根，四面漏风。」满堂登时哄笑起来：「漏勺！漏勺！」褚先生叫道：「沈小满。你说，漏勺能打水吗？」
story.en:
The lecture hall stood east of the main hall, past a stand of old cypresses. On the left-hand door hung a whitewashed wooden board: the timetable. Someone reached "fourth layer and above" and turned to ask, "Is there anybody in this whole room who's on the fourth layer?" Nobody answered.

On the day of the first lecture, the bell had already rung when someone said "Huh?" and pointed out of the window. A streak of green light came slanting down, not fast, like a leaf drifting down on the wind. As it came close they could see it was a man standing on a sword, his grey robe puffed out by the wind. He skimmed over three roof ridges, and of the row of sparrows resting on them not one took fright.

He crooked two fingers back towards himself, and the sword gave a soft ring and slid back of its own accord into the scabbard on his back; he walked in through the door with his hands behind him. The whole hall fell silent at once. Sun Ergou's mouth hung open for a long while, and at last he said softly, "...An immortal."

Sun Ergou held it in for a long while and in the end asked it out loud: "Master Chu, when will we be like you, become immortals, and fly?" Master Chu took a ruler from the lecture table and tapped it twice on his palm, and his goatee twitched. "Become immortals? That's a long way off. But after Foundation Establishment you can ride a sword through the air, and that's not hard." Every eye in the hall lit up.

This was [Master Chu]{注=chuxiansheng}. They said he was fifty or so, but he looked no more than thirty-odd, without a single line in his face. In this whole courtyard he was the only one who had reached Foundation Establishment. Standing on a sword, coming down out of the clouds: he had only one thought left. In this life, I'm going to fly like that, just once. The front few rows were where the true spirit roots sat; the back few were where the false spirit roots and mixed spirit roots sat. Xiaoman sat in the back row.

Master Chu, hands behind his back, wagged his head as he lectured. "One kind: a heavenly spirit root. Two kinds: a true spirit root. Three kinds: a weak spirit root. Four kinds: a false spirit root..." His goatee twitched, and his gaze came to rest squarely on Xiaoman. "All five kinds, what you call a mixed spirit root: leaks on every side." The whole hall burst out laughing: "Leaky ladle! Leaky ladle!" Master Chu called out, "Shen Xiaoman. Tell me, can a leaky ladle draw water?"

story_full.zh:
讲经堂在正殿东边，隔着一片老柏。三开间的一座大屋，青砖到顶，灰瓦，檐角比别的屋子都挑得高，四角各蹲着一只石兽，叫雨淋得没了眉眼；屋脊正当中压着一只小铜鼎，巴掌大，绿锈斑斑。台阶五级，叫三百年的鞋底磨得当中凹下去一道槽，下雨天存得住水。两扇老榆木的门，不上漆，门槛高得要抬腿；门楣上一块匾，黑底，三个字：讲经堂，金漆剥得只剩一半。

左边那扇门上挂着一块刷了白粉的木牌，是课程表，日子不是定死的，执事房隔几天拿炭条改一回。这个月写的是：

**入门课　初三、初九、十六、廿二、廿八，辰时。新入门弟子必到，不得缺席。**

**进阶课　十一、廿五，未时。练气四层以上可听。**

**筑基课　本季一讲，日子另添。练气七层以上可听。**

底下还有一行小字：迟到者，立于廊下听。新弟子们挤在牌子跟前看。有人念到「四层以上」，回头问：「咱们这一屋子，有四层的么？」没有人答。

头一讲那天，钟敲过了，讲堂里的新弟子还在交头接耳，忽然有人「咦」了一声，指着窗外。后山半腰的云，叫什么从里头分开了：一道青光斜斜地落下来，不快，像一片叶子顺着风往下飘。近了，才看清是一个人，脚底下踩着一口剑，一身灰袍叫风鼓起来，两只大袖往后飘着，袍角翻卷，颏下一撮胡子也飘着；他身子四周裹着一层淡淡的白气，像山腰上撕下来的一缕云，跟着他走。他从三重屋脊上头掠过去，屋脊上歇着的一排麻雀一只也没惊起。满堂的人都挤到了窗口，后头的踩着凳子，孙二狗踮着脚，下巴搁在小满肩膀上。

青光在讲堂门口一停，散了。他从剑上下来，脚落地，没有一点声音；那身鼓着的袍子，这才慢慢地垂了下来。砖缝里渗出来的那层白气，本来贴着地皮懒懒地流，这时候一齐往他脚边涌过去，绕着他的鞋打了个旋儿，像一群见了主人的狗。他两根手指往回一招，那口剑「铮」地轻吟一声，自己缩回他背后的鞘里；他背着手进了门。满堂一下子没了声。坐在门边的几个，后颈上的汗毛先立了起来，像冬天推门，迎面一股冷气——又不是冷，是满屋的灵气都往他身上去了。不知是谁先站了起来，跟着一屋子人全站了起来，凳子腿刮着砖地，「吱吱嘎嘎」响成一片。孙二狗嘴张着，半天没合上，末了小声道：「……神仙。」前排一个姑娘，两只手攥在胸口。第一排的马小宝，不知不觉把腰挺得笔直。

孙二狗憋了半天，到底问出了口：「褚先生，何时我们才能像您一样，成仙，会飞啊？」褚先生从讲桌上拿起戒尺，在掌心里拍了两下，山羊胡子翘了一翘：「成仙？还早着呢。不过筑基之后，便可御剑飞行，这个倒不难。只需你们按时来听课，回去勤加练习。」满堂的眼睛都亮了。

这便是[褚先生]{注=chuxiansheng}。听说五十来岁了，看着不过三十许，脸上一条褶子也没有，只颏下一撮山羊胡子，生得精瘦，在讲经堂讲了三十年经；这一院子里，只他一个是筑了基的，旁人身上落一层灰，他那件灰袍，灰都落不上去。小满在最后一排，偷偷看了一眼自己的袖口，又看了一眼那件灰袍。踩着一口剑，从云里下来——他心里只剩一句话：这辈子，我也要这么飞上一回。

讲经堂的地底下，压着一道细细的灵脉，砖缝里一早一晚渗出一点白气，贴着地皮流，流到前头几排，还有膝盖高，流到后头，只剩一层薄霜似的影子。前头几排坐的是真灵根，后头几排坐的是伪灵根、杂灵根，这是谁也没定过的规矩，可谁都照着坐。小满坐在最后一排，孙二狗坐在他左边，马小宝凭着荐书，坐在第一排。

褚先生背着手，摇头晃脑地讲道：「天地之间，灵气充盈。凡人不能纳，修士能纳。何也？——灵根也。一门者，天灵根；二门者，真灵根；三门者，弱灵根；四门者，伪灵根——」山羊胡子一翘，目光不偏不倚停在小满身上，「——五门俱全的，你们叫杂灵根，四面漏风。」满堂登时哄笑起来，有人拿指头在桌上敲着节拍：「漏勺！漏勺！」褚先生叫道：「沈小满。你说，漏勺能打水吗？」
story_full.en:
The lecture hall stood east of the main hall, past a stand of old cypresses. A big building three bays wide, grey brick to the roof, grey tiles, its eave corners lifted higher than any other building's, a stone beast crouched on each of the four, their faces worn away by rain. In the middle of the roof ridge sat a little bronze cauldron, palm-sized, mottled with verdigris. Five steps up, worn by three hundred years of shoe soles into a groove down the middle that held water when it rained. Two doors of old elm, unpainted, with a threshold so high you had to lift your leg. Over the doors hung a board, black ground, three characters: Lecture Hall, the gold lacquer flaked down to half.

On the left-hand door hung a whitewashed wooden board: the timetable. The days weren't fixed; the stewards' office changed it in charcoal every few days. This month it said:

**Entry Classes: 3rd, 9th, 16th, 22nd, 28th, hour of the Dragon. New disciples must attend. No absence permitted.**

**Advanced Classes: 11th, 25th, hour of the Goat. Open to fourth layer of Qi Condensation and above.**

**Foundation Classes: one lecture this season, date to be added. Open to seventh layer of Qi Condensation and above.**

Below that was a line in small writing: latecomers stand in the corridor to listen. The new disciples crowded in front of the board to read it. Someone reached "fourth layer and above" and turned to ask, "Is there anybody in this whole room who's on the fourth layer?" Nobody answered.

On the day of the first lecture, the bell had already rung and the new disciples in the hall were still whispering when someone said "Huh?" and pointed out of the window. The cloud halfway up the back of the mountain was being parted by something inside it: a streak of green light came slanting down, not fast, like a leaf drifting down on the wind. As it came close they could see it was a man standing on a sword, his grey robe puffed out by the wind, his two big sleeves streaming behind him, the corners of his robe flapping, the tuft of beard on his chin streaming too. All round him was wrapped a faint white haze, like a wisp of cloud torn off the mountainside, following him. He skimmed over three roof ridges, and of the row of sparrows resting on them not one took fright. Everyone in the hall crowded to the windows; those at the back stood on stools, and Sun Ergou, on tiptoe, rested his chin on Xiaoman's shoulder.

The green light stopped at the door of the lecture hall and scattered. He stepped down from the sword, and his feet touched the ground without a sound; only then did the puffed-out robe slowly fall still. The white haze seeping from between the bricks, which had been flowing lazily along the ground, now all surged to his feet together and swirled once round his shoes like a pack of dogs that had seen their master. He crooked two fingers back towards himself, and the sword gave a soft ring and slid back of its own accord into the scabbard on his back; he walked in through the door with his hands behind him. The whole hall fell silent at once. The few sitting by the door felt the hairs on the backs of their necks stand up first, like opening a door in winter into a blast of cold air. Except it wasn't cold. It was all the spirit qi in the room going to him. Someone, no one knew who, stood up first, and then the whole room stood, stool legs scraping on the brick floor in a long creaking racket. Sun Ergou's mouth hung open for a long while, and at last he said softly, "...An immortal." A girl in the front row held both hands clasped to her chest. Ma Xiaobao in the first row had, without noticing, sat up dead straight.

Sun Ergou held it in for a long while and in the end asked it out loud: "Master Chu, when will we be like you, become immortals, and fly?" Master Chu took a ruler from the lecture table and tapped it twice on his palm, and his goatee twitched. "Become immortals? That's a long way off. But after Foundation Establishment you can ride a sword through the air, and that's not hard. You only need to come to class on time and practise hard when you go back." Every eye in the hall lit up.

This was [Master Chu]{注=chuxiansheng}. They said he was fifty or so, but he looked no more than thirty-odd, without a single line in his face, only a goatee tuft under his chin. He was lean and wiry, and had been lecturing in the lecture hall for thirty years; in this whole courtyard he was the only one who had reached Foundation Establishment. Everyone else had a layer of dust on them; on that grey robe of his, dust wouldn't even settle. Xiaoman, in the back row, stole a look at his own cuffs, then at that grey robe. Standing on a sword, coming down out of the clouds: he had only one thought left. In this life, I'm going to fly like that, just once.

Under the floor of the lecture hall ran a thin vein of spirit qi, and morning and evening a little white haze seeped up between the bricks and flowed along the ground. By the front few rows it was still knee-high; by the back it was only a shadow like a thin frost. The front few rows were where the true spirit roots sat; the back few were where the false spirit roots and mixed spirit roots sat. Nobody had ever made it a rule, but everybody sat that way. Xiaoman sat in the back row with Sun Ergou on his left; Ma Xiaobao, on the strength of his letter, sat in the first row.

Master Chu, hands behind his back, wagged his head as he lectured. "Between heaven and earth, spirit qi is everywhere. Ordinary people cannot take it in. Cultivators can. Why? Because of the spirit root. One kind: a heavenly spirit root. Two kinds: a true spirit root. Three kinds: a weak spirit root. Four kinds: a false spirit root..." His goatee twitched, and his gaze came to rest squarely on Xiaoman. "All five kinds, what you call a mixed spirit root: leaks on every side." The whole hall burst out laughing, and someone beat time on the desk with his fingers: "Leaky ladle! Leaky ladle!" Master Chu called out, "Shen Xiaoman. Tell me, can a leaky ladle draw water?"

exits.means: answers that a leaky ladle can carry water — by going back more times

story.zh:
小满说：「能打。」满堂都是一愣，褚先生也愣了，半晌才道：「……怎么打？」小满说：「多打几次。」

满堂又笑了，后头几排的杂灵根们却不回头，一个个低着头，肩膀一抽一抽的。胸口的木牌里，一个又困又不耐烦的声音在他耳朵里道：「……谁在吵？」他压低了头：「先生说杂灵根是漏勺。」那声音哼了一声：「他懂个屁。」

褚先生把戒尺在讲桌上一敲：「多打几次。好。《列子》上有个愚公，带着儿孙一筐一筐挑土。——后来呢？天帝感他的诚，派两个大力神，把山背走了。」他拿戒尺朝最后一排一指，「诸位记着：山，是神仙背走的。沈小满，你家里有子子孙孙替你挖么？你有神仙么？」

话到了舌尖，一个「藏」字压了下去。他道：「……没有。」褚先生道：「那就记着：漏勺，便是漏勺。坐下。」这一回，后排没有一个人低头笑。
story.en:
Xiaoman said, "It can." The whole hall was taken aback. Master Chu was taken aback too, and only after a long moment said, "...How?" Xiaoman said, "Draw it more times."

The whole hall laughed again; the mixed roots in the back few rows didn't turn round. They kept their heads down, and their shoulders shook. From the wooden tablet at his chest a sleepy, impatient voice said in his ear, "...Who's making a racket?" He bent his head. "The master says mixed spirit roots are leaky ladles." The voice snorted. "He knows nothing."

Master Chu rapped the ruler on the lecture table. "Draw it more times. Good. In the *Liezi* there's a Foolish Old Man, who set about carrying the earth away basket by basket with his sons and grandsons. And then what? The Emperor of Heaven was moved by his sincerity and sent two giants to carry the mountains away on their backs." He pointed the ruler at the back row. "Remember this, all of you: the mountains were carried off by gods. Shen Xiaoman, have you got sons and grandsons at home to dig for you? Have you got a god?"

The words were on the tip of his tongue, and one word held them down: hide. He said, "...No." Master Chu said, "Then remember: a leaky ladle is a leaky ladle. Sit down." This time nobody in the back rows bent their heads and laughed.

story_full.zh:
小满说：「能打。」

满堂都是一愣，褚先生也愣了，山羊胡子翘在半空里，半晌才道：「……怎么打？」

小满说：「多打几次。」

满堂又笑了，只是这一回笑的方向，跟方才有点不一样：前头几排回过头来瞧他，像瞧一个说胡话的傻子；后头几排的杂灵根们却不回头，一个个低着头，肩膀一抽一抽的。小满坐下，胸口的木牌里，一个又困又不耐烦的声音在他耳朵里道：「……谁在吵？」他压低了头：「先生说杂灵根是漏勺。」那声音哼了一声：「他懂个屁。」

褚先生却不恼。这四个字，每三年开一回山门，他总要听见一回。他把戒尺在讲桌上一敲：「多打几次。好。《列子》上有个愚公，快九十岁了，嫌两座大山挡了家门，带着儿孙一筐一筐挑土。邻家的智叟笑他，他说：我死了，还有儿子；儿子又生孙子，子子孙孙没有穷尽，山却不会再长高。——后来呢？天帝感他的诚，派两个大力神，把山背走了。」他拿戒尺朝最后一排一指，「诸位记着：山，是神仙背走的。愚公挖了一辈子，挖下来几筐土？沈小满，你家里有子子孙孙替你挖么？你有神仙么？」

前头几排又笑了。小满张了张嘴。木牌里方才还骂过一句「他懂个屁」。话到了舌尖，一个「藏」字压了下去。他道：「……没有。」

褚先生道：「那就记着：漏勺，便是漏勺。坐下。」

这一回，后排没有一个人低头笑。
story_full.en:
Xiaoman said, "It can."

The whole hall was taken aback. Master Chu was taken aback too, his goatee stuck in mid-twitch, and only after a long moment said, "...How?"

Xiaoman said, "Draw it more times."

The whole hall laughed again, only this time the laughter went a slightly different way from before. The front few rows turned round to look at him, the way you look at a fool talking nonsense; the mixed roots in the back few rows didn't turn round. They kept their heads down, and their shoulders shook. Xiaoman sat down, and from the wooden tablet at his chest a sleepy, impatient voice said in his ear, "...Who's making a racket?" He bent his head. "The master says mixed spirit roots are leaky ladles." The voice snorted. "He knows nothing."

Master Chu wasn't annoyed, though. Those four words, every three years when the gate opened, he always heard once. He rapped the ruler on the lecture table. "Draw it more times. Good. In the *Liezi* there's a Foolish Old Man, nearly ninety, who was tired of two great mountains blocking his door and set about carrying the earth away basket by basket with his sons and grandsons. The Wise Old Man next door laughed at him, and he said: when I die, there'll be my sons; my sons will have grandsons, sons and grandsons without end, and the mountains won't grow any taller. And then what? The Emperor of Heaven was moved by his sincerity and sent two giants to carry the mountains away on their backs." He pointed the ruler at the back row. "Remember this, all of you: the mountains were carried off by gods. The Foolish Old Man dug his whole life, and how many baskets of earth did he get down? Shen Xiaoman, have you got sons and grandsons at home to dig for you? Have you got a god?"

The front few rows laughed again. Xiaoman opened his mouth. A moment ago the tablet had said "He knows nothing." The words were on the tip of his tongue, and one word held them down: hide. He said, "...No."

Master Chu said, "Then remember: a leaky ladle is a leaky ladle. Sit down."

This time nobody in the back rows bent their heads and laughed.
